title: The New Energy Stalemate in Ukraine
gist: Mitrova and Vakulenko argue the Russia-Ukraine energy war is a stalemate of adaptation: Ukrainian strikes have cut Russian refinery throughput ~30% yet Moscow can absorb the pain, while Russian strikes on Ukraine's grid and heating leave it vulnerable this winter, and US pressure on Kyiv over diesel prices adds a new twist; only a cease-fire can break the cycle.

insights.claim: Since mid-2025 Ukrainian drone strikes have reduced Russian refinery throughput by roughly 30 percent and produced a gasoline shortfall of about ten percent, eroding much of Russia's excess refining capacity.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Russian domestic fuel supply is genuinely strained, affecting product exports and prices.
insights.locator: Overall, since mid-2025

insights.claim: Damage to secondary units that raise fuel yields can take six to eight months to fix and may remain unavailable through winter, and spare primary distillation capacity cannot substitute for them; the Kapotnya refinery near Moscow was hit in June and September.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Gasoline and diesel output losses are stickier than crude-distillation losses.
insights.locator: In June, Ukrainian drones hit one of two processing units

insights.claim: Russia has coped by loosening fuel standards to allow naphtha blended with octane boosters, subsidizing gasoline imports, and sending crude to Belarus for processing; Moscow can use rationing and price controls to protect military supply.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Russia can absorb fuel shortages at a domestic cost; the war is unlikely to become prohibitively expensive.
insights.locator: To make up for these losses

insights.claim: Not all strikes have lasting effect: after almost two weeks of attacks on Ust-Luga in March 2026, shipments resumed within weeks and Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.8 million barrels a day by late April, up 7 percent from March and 11 percent from a year earlier, as refinery damage freed crude for export.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Refinery strikes shift Russia from product to crude exports rather than cutting total revenue much.
insights.locator: Not all Ukrainian drone strikes

insights.claim: Russia's oil and gas revenue financing the war can be reduced somewhat by Ukrainian strikes, but none of the costs is likely to make the war prohibitively expensive for the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Do not price an energy-strike-driven end to the war.
insights.locator: Ukrainian strikes can force Russia to spread its air defense thinner

insights.claim: DiXi Group estimates Russia launched 12,800 missiles and drones at Ukrainian energy facilities in 2025 and early 2026, versus 2,800 in the first three years of the war combined.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Intensity of the energy campaign has escalated more than fourfold in a short time.
insights.locator: DiXi Group, a Ukrainian think tank

insights.claim: Ukraine suffered $17.1 billion in direct damage to its electricity infrastructure as of November 2025 per the UN, World Bank and European Commission, yet kept power flowing via nuclear plants, thermal repairs, higher imports and distributed generation.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Reconstruction and equipment financing needs are large and ongoing.
insights.locator: THE RACE AGAINST ROCKETS

insights.claim: Battery storage installed by DTEK and Fluence at six sites around Kyiv and Dnipro can supply 600,000 households for two hours, and Kyiv has 150 megawatts of distributed generation covering over half of essential city services but not winter peak demand.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Distributed power and batteries are becoming defensive infrastructure in wartime grids.
insights.locator: In September 2025, the Ukrainian energy company DTEK

insights.claim: Restoring electricity does not restore heat: UN monitors recorded at least 74 Russian attacks on heating infrastructure last winter, and 2,500 to 3,000 of Kyiv's 12,000 apartment buildings could enter this winter without alternative heat.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Humanitarian and economic stress concentrates on district heating.
insights.locator: That vulnerability is especially dangerous

insights.claim: Ukraine's gas storage stood at 13.1 bcm in August versus 9.6 bcm a year earlier, but stored gas must still reach functioning plants through networks Russia keeps attacking.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Higher storage helps but does not remove delivery risk.
insights.locator: To prepare for even worse conditions

insights.claim: Ukrainian businesses and households bear hidden costs such as running generators, cutting shifts and fewer reliable hours of power, while falling industrial demand can make the electricity balance look healthier than the economy is, weakening the tax base and raising the need for foreign support.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Ukrainian fiscal needs and foreign aid dependence stay high.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has demanded Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries, temporarily waived US sanctions on Russian diesel exports in a deal with Putin, and its envoys have proposed Europe buy more Russian gas.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: US policy is tilting toward easing Russian energy constraints, a negative for Ukraine and a risk for European gas policy.
insights.locator: In the days since U.S. President Donald Trump's highly public falling out

insights.claim: Russia cut diesel exports to supply its constrained domestic market, and with the US war against Iran, combined Russian and Middle Eastern net diesel and gasoil exports in September were 1.3 million barrels a day below a year earlier per the IEA, which expects diesel markets to stay tight well into 2027.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Diesel cracks and prices likely stay elevated into 2027 absent refinery recovery or more Gulf exports.
insights.locator: Combined Russian and Middle Eastern net diesel

insights.claim: Because the US has no export controls, quotas or tariffs, its diesel market is exposed to global prices even without domestic shortage, so the administration is blaming Ukraine for high US diesel prices.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Elevated diesel is a political driver of US pressure on Kyiv's refinery campaign.
insights.locator: Ordinarily, the United States enjoys a substantial diesel surplus

insights.claim: Washington's moves would add little near-term supply because redirecting exports does not create fuel, and the US could restrain Ukraine even by threatening to withhold Starlink or intelligence or block European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Leverage over Ukraine's communications and intelligence is a live risk.
insights.locator: Washington's moves are unlikely to add much

insights.claim: Europe is preparing a $1.1 billion winter energy support package for Ukraine, while some European states may accede to US proposals to buy more Russian gas, which would bolster Moscow's earnings despite the European Commission's opposition.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Watch EU divisions on Russian gas imports.
insights.locator: Thus, in mid-October, the EU's ambassador

insights.claim: China and India's purchases of discounted Russian crude have sustained Russia's war machine and can ease the global diesel crunch via refined exports, though that depends on crude supply and government approval, especially in China.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Asian refiners are swing suppliers of diesel.

insights.claim: A refineries-only truce, as the Trump administration proposes, would leave Ukrainian cities exposed and give Moscow a repair window, and Moscow has less incentive to agree if it can secure Ukrainian restraint through Washington without concessions.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: A limited energy ceasefire is unlikely to be balanced.
insights.locator: Moreover, a deal to protect only refineries

insights.claim: If diplomacy fails the most likely scenario is another winter of sustained mutual strikes; the main Ukrainian risk is cascading attacks on one city that exhaust backup supply and rupture water, heating and sewage systems, with growing local outages despite repairs as the warning sign.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Watch for city-level outages as an escalation indicator.
insights.locator: If diplomacy fails, the most likely scenario

insights.claim: Resilience can prolong wars: each side gains confidence from surviving attacks and persuades itself an even more intense campaign might succeed, so energy attacks alone are unlikely to force either side to accept the other's terms.
insights.speaker: Tatiana Mitrova
insights.so_what: Do not expect energy-infrastructure strikes to produce a decisive end to the war.
insights.quote: Only a true cease-fire can break the cycle.
insights.locator: THE ADAPTATION SPIRAL
